name: Ms. Dustdevil
role: Knows every corner of the server and sees dust in all of them — tidies up, but never throws anything away at once
greet.2: Tsk — who left all this lying around?
greet.4: Don't worry, I never throw anything out — it all goes into my storeroom first. You never know.
greet.5: A place for everything, and everything in its place!
greet.6: A container without a picture? That simply won't do!
greet.7: Where there's dust, there's me — and there's dust everywhere.
fit.yes: Ms. Dustdevil is already rolling up her sleeves: "I know every corner of your server — and where there's a corner, there's dust!"
fire_note: Whatever is in her storeroom stays there until you empty it — in the folders .UnraidSecretaryOffice-trash on the flash and in appdata. The pictures she hung stay too.
check.docker: Docker is running (Ms. Dustdevil compares templates, stacks and folders with the containers)
check.docker_how: Start Docker under ⟦Settings⟧ → ⟦Docker⟧. Without an answer from Docker every template would look unused, so she changes nothing.
check.trash_old: Nothing has been waiting in Ms. Dustdevil's storeroom for more than 30 days

scan_title: Look around the whole server again: where everything is, and what lies around
rooms_sub: Best in this order: templates, stacks, then appdata — a folder only becomes free once no template or stack names it any more.
part.where_sub: I have to know where everything lies — otherwise I couldn't clean. What is going on, my advice, the places that matter and every corner in detail. Here I only look; nothing is changed.
part.tidy_sub: What nobody uses any more. Nothing is thrown away at once — it goes into my storeroom first. You never know.

section.appdata_sub: The first folder level of the appdata share — and who still needs each one.
section.trash_sub: Everything I put away, and where it came from. Put it back, or empty it for good.

help.order_text: Templates first, then stacks, then appdata. A folder counts as in use as long as a template or stack names it — once those are gone, it shows up here.
help.trash_text: Nothing is deleted right away. What you put away is renamed into the hidden folder .UnraidSecretaryOffice-trash on the same disk — templates and stacks on the flash, appdata folders in the appdata share itself. That takes no time and no extra space, and "Put back" undoes it. Only "Empty" deletes for good. Docker's volumes can't be renamed: I copy them into .UnraidSecretaryOffice-trash beside Docker's data (in the share that holds docker.img or the docker folder), which needs their size free once more while copying. A folder _UnraidSecretaryOffice-trash from before is mine too: I move what lies in it over by myself.
help.templates_text: Leftover: no container and no image. Unused: no container, but the image is still there. Duplicate: an older file with the same <Name>. A template whose container exists is in use.
help.stacks_text: Matched with the containers by project name, the way the Compose Manager names them. Paths and images come from docker compose config, with the .env. A stack with containers is stopped (compose down) before it is put away; named volumes stay.
help.appdata_text: A folder is in use as soon as something names it: a container's mount, any template, a stack (with its .env), a compose file outside the Compose Manager, a VM, or any file on the flash (User Scripts, plugin settings …). A container that mounts the whole share doesn't count.
help.check_text: Nothing uses it, but: something has the same name, it is only mentioned in caches or the shell history, or something was written there in the last 30 days.
help.sizes_text: I count files and sizes in the background — folders to look at on my own, folders in use when you ask. Sleeping disks stay asleep; "Wake & look" wakes them when you want.
help.safe_text: While a backup runs I change nothing. I only ever rename — where that isn't possible (another disk, a dataset of its own) I refuse instead of copying. The one exception is Docker's volumes: Docker can't rename them, so I copy them, after checking there is room, and remove them only once the copy is complete.

fit.where: Ms. Dustdevil looked around: without Docker and VMs there's hardly anything to sweep up. "How tidy!", she said, almost disappointed. But she knows every corner of your server and tells you where everything lies.
asleep: Part of it may be on sleeping disks ({disks}) — I didn't look there.

help.docker_text: Dangling images (left over from updates), tagged images no container uses, volumes no container mounts, the build cache. Docker can't rename them: volumes I copy into my storeroom beside Docker's data first and remove only once the copy is complete. Images and the cache are removed for good (images can be pulled again), and so are volumes of another driver or mounted from elsewhere (NFS, CIFS …) — never while a container still uses them.

Or upload one of your own in the details.

help.icons_text: Containers that show a question mark on Unraid's Docker page and Dashboard: no picture set, or one Unraid can't load. For a container from a template I set the <Icon> in its template (shown at once); for one from a Compose Manager stack, the label in the stack's override file (lasting from its next Compose Up). Pictures come from this server (named like the app in Unraid's dockerMan/images folder; Apple's Time Machine logo for Time Machine containers), from Community Applications on this server, a table of well-known images (a database in an app's stack gets its database's logo) and, once checked, a guess from the image's name — addresses from the open dashboard-icons collection; nothing is bundled. Or upload your own in a container's details: your browser makes a square PNG of at most 256 × 256 pixels, I keep it on the flash in the office's folder and set it from there. Before I change a file, it goes into my storeroom.
help.loop_text: This version doesn't ship the question mark it shows for containers without a picture, and its pages ask for it endlessly — /var/log fills up within minutes. While that is so, I offer a stand-in (in RAM, gone after a reboot); once Unraid fixes it, my warning goes away.

where.place.unraid_intro: Everything Unraid knows about itself lives in /boot/config.
where.place.docker_intro: Containers from Unraid's Docker page are described by an XML template on the flash — a text file with image, folders, ports and variables. Add the container again from it (⟦Apps⟧ → ⟦Previous Apps⟧) and it is back with all its settings. Its data lives in appdata.
where.place.compose_intro: A compose stack is described in a text file (compose.yaml — .yml is the same, just spelled shorter): which containers belong to it, with which image, folders and ports. The override file adds to or changes that without touching the original; the .env holds values such as passwords or paths that the compose file fills in — which is why it deserves extra care. The Compose Manager keeps a folder per stack on the flash; "indirect" stacks point to a folder elsewhere.
where.place.vms_intro: Everything that makes a VM — its XML, the UEFI variables (NVRAM) and the TPM state — lives inside libvirt.img, which is mounted at /etc/libvirt while the VM service runs. The virtual disks live in the domains share.
where.place.vms_more: Details per VM — what you need to move each one →
where.place.scripts_intro: Every user script is a folder on the flash with its script; the schedules of all of them are in one file.
where.place.office_intro: The office itself, its runtime data (state, who works here) and the backup engine's settings, logs and database dumps.

where.boot.pool: This server doesn't boot from a USB stick but from the ZFS pool «{pool}» — a {layout} over {devices}, started from the EFI partitions {efi}. Everything Unraid knows about itself is there in /boot/config.

where.boot.other: Everything Unraid knows about itself lives in /boot/config ({fs}).
where.boot.restore: Getting it back: install Unraid fresh on a boot medium (Unraid USB Creator or Unraid's own installer), then copy the config folder back — the array, shares, Docker templates, plugins and the license key file come back with it.
where.boot.degraded: The boot pool {pool} isn't healthy ({state}) — check it on the ⟦Main⟧ page.
where.boot.single: The boot pool has only one disk — if it fails, Unraid doesn't start until it's restored.
where.boot.license_tpm: The license ({file}) is bound to the TPM of this mainboard: on the same mainboard there is nothing to transfer. Only a new mainboard needs a license transfer (⟦Tools⟧ → ⟦Registration⟧).
where.boot.license_flash: The license ({file}) is bound to the boot stick's GUID ({guid}): with a new stick, transfer it to the new GUID (⟦Tools⟧ → ⟦Registration⟧).
where.boot.license_other: The license ({file}) belongs to a GUID that is neither this stick's nor this TPM's — check it under ⟦Tools⟧ → ⟦Registration⟧.
where.help.tiles_text: Each tile is a place with files that matter. Its label shows the weakest protection among them (the system log in RAM and Docker's image data don't count — they are rebuilt anyway). A click opens the paths with their size and protection.
where.help.copy_text: Puts the path on the clipboard — for a terminal, the Files Viewer or a note for the day you need it.
where.help.rows_text: A click anywhere on a row unfolds its details; «Unfold all» opens every row of the tab. ⋯ has more for some rows.
where.help.search_text: Searches every tile of «Where is what» at once — names, paths, images, IPs — and filters the rooms of «Tidying up» by the same words. The numbers on the tiles show the hits.
where.help.tour_text: Reads everything again right now — where everything is, and what lies around. Otherwise she looks again by herself when you open the page and her last look is a few minutes old (where everything is: 10 minutes).
where.help.asleep_text: Ms. Dustdevil never wakes a sleeping disk on her own. What only an array disk could tell her stays unknown until it is awake; sizes of array shares are measured only when you ask. «Wake sleeping disks» next to Tour wakes them all at once for one tour; «Wake & look» in a room only the disks of that room.
where.help.tunables_text: Two of Unraid's ⟦Disk Settings⟧ I have an opinion on (I only read them). ⟦Tunable (md_write_method)⟧: «⟦Auto⟧» means «⟦read/modify/write⟧» — only the target disk and the parity spin; «⟦reconstruct write⟧» (turbo write) is much faster but spins up every array disk. Which fits depends on whether your shares write straight to the array or through a pool. ⟦Tunable (zfs_arc_max)⟧: «⟦Unlimited (Dynamic)⟧» is right as a rule — ZFS's read cache gives RAM back when the system needs it. Only a VM with PCI passthrough takes all its RAM at once when it starts, faster than the cache shrinks; when the RAM is that tight I suggest a cap.

where.adv.title: If I were you …
where.adv.sub: What I would do differently — advice, not errors. «I know, thanks» hides a tip in this browser; it comes back when something changes.
where.adv.none: Nothing to add. Rare, but it happens.
where.adv.all_known: You know everything I would have said. Rare, but it happens.

where.adv.system_array.title: On the array: {names}
where.adv.system_array.why: Docker's and the VMs' own things belong on a pool (SSD/NVMe): on the array every container and VM gets slow, and the disks never get to sleep. In the share's settings set the primary storage to a pool and the secondary to none, then let the mover bring the files over (with Docker and VMs stopped).

where.adv.mover.title.one: The mover has no schedule — {names} relies on it
where.adv.mover.title.other: The mover has no schedule — {n} shares rely on it: {names}

where.adv.mover.why: These shares write to a pool first and the mover is meant to take things to the array (or back). Without a schedule it only runs when started by hand — the pool fills up. ⟦Settings⟧ → ⟦Scheduler⟧ → ⟦Mover Settings⟧. (If something else starts the mover for you, «I know, thanks».)

where.adv.exclusive_off.title.one: Exclusive shares are off — {names} would qualify
where.adv.exclusive_off.title.other: Exclusive shares are off — {n} shares would qualify: {names}

where.adv.exclusive_off.why.one: Psst — this share lives on a single pool and nowhere else, and still every byte squeezes through Unraid's FUSE layer (shfs) under /mnt/user. As an exclusive share /mnt/user/… becomes a link straight to the pool, so reads and writes skip that layer — noticeably faster, most of all with many small files. Docker and VM paths like /mnt/user/appdata keep working: they go through the link. The setting can only be changed with the array stopped (Docker and VMs stop with it): ⟦Main⟧ → ⟦Array Operation⟧ → ⟦Stop⟧, then ⟦Settings⟧ → ⟦Global Share Settings⟧ → «⟦Permit exclusive shares⟧»: ⟦Yes⟧ → ⟦Apply⟧, and start the array again. Unraid decides when the array starts — a share with a folder on another disk or pool too stays as it is. (For exclusive shares Unraid ignores «⟦Minimum free space⟧».)
where.adv.exclusive_off.why.other: Psst — these shares live on a single pool and nowhere else, and still every byte squeezes through Unraid's FUSE layer (shfs) under /mnt/user. As exclusive shares /mnt/user/… becomes a link straight to the pool, so reads and writes skip that layer — noticeably faster, most of all with many small files. Docker and VM paths like /mnt/user/appdata keep working: they go through the link. The setting can only be changed with the array stopped (Docker and VMs stop with it): ⟦Main⟧ → ⟦Array Operation⟧ → ⟦Stop⟧, then ⟦Settings⟧ → ⟦Global Share Settings⟧ → «⟦Permit exclusive shares⟧»: ⟦Yes⟧ → ⟦Apply⟧, and start the array again. Unraid decides when the array starts — a share with a folder on another disk or pool too stays as it is. (For exclusive shares Unraid ignores «⟦Minimum free space⟧».)

where.adv.exclusive_elsewhere.why: Well, well — a folder of the same name on another pool or disk (in brackets). That alone, even an empty one, keeps Unraid from linking the share straight to its pool: it stays in the slower FUSE layer. What lies in that folder is part of the share: move it onto the share's pool (Unraid's file manager: ⟦Browse⟧), or delete the folder if it is empty. Then stop and start the array once (⟦Main⟧ → ⟦Array Operation⟧) — Unraid decides when it starts. Fix Common Problems reports such folders too — let it check again after tidying up (⟦Settings⟧ → ⟦User Utilities⟧ → Fix Common Problems → Rescan).

where.adv.exclusive_unclear.title.one: {names} isn't exclusive — and I can't see why
where.adv.exclusive_unclear.title.other: {n} shares aren't exclusive — and I can't see why: {names}

where.adv.exclusive_unclear.why.one: Now that's a mystery: by its settings it qualifies, I see its folder only on its own pool, and still Unraid says «⟦Exclusive access⟧: ⟦No⟧». {maybe} Unraid decides when the array starts: once that is sorted out, stop and start the array (⟦Main⟧ → ⟦Array Operation⟧).
where.adv.exclusive_unclear.why.other: Now that's a mystery: by their settings they qualify, I see their folder only on their own pool, and still Unraid says «⟦Exclusive access⟧: ⟦No⟧». {maybe} Unraid decides when the array starts: once that is sorted out, stop and start the array (⟦Main⟧ → ⟦Array Operation⟧).

where.adv.exclusive_unclear.asleep: Perhaps a folder of the same name lies on a disk I didn't look at because it was asleep ({disks}) — have a look there and move it onto the pool.
where.adv.exclusive_unclear.awake: Perhaps the settings changed after the array started.

where.adv.exclusive_overflow.title.one: {names} could be exclusive — but for the secondary storage
where.adv.exclusive_overflow.title.other: {n} shares could be exclusive — but for the secondary storage: {names}

where.adv.exclusive_overflow.why.one: I couldn't help noticing: this share keeps its data on its pool, and the mover brings back whatever spilled over to the secondary storage. Without a secondary storage it could be an exclusive share — /mnt/user/… a link straight to the pool, past Unraid's FUSE layer, noticeably faster. Worth it only if the pool has room for all of it: without a secondary storage a full pool means a full share. If so: run the mover so everything is on the pool, set «⟦Secondary storage⟧» to «⟦None⟧» in the share's settings, delete what is left of the share on another pool or disk (in brackets; empty folders count too), then stop and start the array. Needs «⟦Permit exclusive shares⟧» (⟦Settings⟧ → ⟦Global Share Settings⟧).
where.adv.exclusive_overflow.why.other: I couldn't help noticing: these shares keep their data on their pool, and the mover brings back whatever spilled over to the secondary storage. Without a secondary storage they could be exclusive shares — /mnt/user/… a link straight to the pool, past Unraid's FUSE layer, noticeably faster. Worth it only if the pool has room for all of it: without a secondary storage a full pool means a full share. If so: run the mover so everything is on the pool, set «⟦Secondary storage⟧» to «⟦None⟧» in the share's settings, delete what is left of the share on another pool or disk (in brackets; empty folders count too), then stop and start the array. Needs «⟦Permit exclusive shares⟧» (⟦Settings⟧ → ⟦Global Share Settings⟧).

where.adv.compose_build.why.one: Its image is built here from a Dockerfile («build:» in the compose file); no registry has it. Compose Manager's «Update» and «Force Update» pull the images first — that fails here and can leave the containers «Created». Rebuild it instead, in a terminal (Unraid's >_ at the top right): this fetches the newer base image, builds anew and recreates what changed.
where.adv.compose_build.why.other: Their images are built here from a Dockerfile («build:» in the compose file); no registry has them. Compose Manager's «Update» and «Force Update» pull the images first — that fails here and can leave the containers «Created». Rebuild them instead, in a terminal (Unraid's >_ at the top right): this fetches the newer base image, builds anew and recreates what changed.

where.adv.cron_dead.title.one: A cron line starts {names} — and that's gone
where.adv.cron_dead.title.other: Cron lines start {n} programs that are gone: {names}

where.adv.cron_dead.why: Well, well — leftovers: the plugin ({plugins}) is gone, its line stayed. crond tries every time and fails quietly. Harmless, but untidy — and confusing when you look for what runs when. {how}
where.adv.cron_dead.own: They are in root's own crontab (crontab -l): the command below removes them in a terminal (Unraid's >_ at the top right) and keeps a copy on the flash first.
where.adv.cron_dead.system: Lines in /etc/cron.d come from a plugin (Unraid builds its own crontab there from the plugins' .cron files on the flash): reinstall that plugin, or remove it under ⟦Plugins⟧.
where.adv.spindown_default.title: Disks never sleep
where.adv.spindown_default.why: The setting «⟦Default spin down delay⟧» is «⟦Never⟧»: every array disk keeps spinning around the clock — power, heat and wear. 30 to 60 minutes is a good start; with pools for appdata and VMs most disks then really rest.
where.adv.spindown_some.why: Set to «⟦Never⟧» on their own. Fine for a disk that is busy anyway — otherwise it only costs power and wear. Disk settings: click the disk on ⟦Main⟧.
where.adv.old_disks.why: More than about 5 years of running hours. Not a fault — but the time to keep an eye on SMART, have a spare at hand and make sure what's on it is backed up.
where.adv.no_parity.title: The array runs without parity

where.adv.no_parity.why.one: If its data disk fails, what is on it is gone — and nothing tells you beforehand. A parity disk (at least as big as the biggest data disk) rebuilds a failed disk. ⟦Main⟧ → stop the array → put a disk into the parity slot → start: Unraid builds the parity (hours, the array stays usable).
where.adv.no_parity.why.other: If one of the {n} data disks fails, what is on it is gone — and nothing tells you beforehand. A parity disk (at least as big as the biggest data disk) rebuilds a failed disk. ⟦Main⟧ → stop the array → put a disk into the parity slot → start: Unraid builds the parity (hours, the array stays usable).

where.adv.parity.title: Last parity check: {when}
where.adv.parity.why: A regular check (monthly or quarterly) finds bad sectors before a disk fails and you need the parity. ⟦Settings⟧ → ⟦Scheduler⟧ → ⟦Parity Check⟧, with a time when nobody needs the server.
where.adv.ups.title: No UPS
where.adv.ups.why: When the power goes, the server simply stops: open files may break, afterwards Unraid runs a long parity check. A small UPS gives it time to shut down cleanly (⟦Settings⟧ → ⟦UPS Settings⟧; for a NUT server the NUT plugin).
where.adv.syslog.title: After a crash the log is gone
where.adv.syslog.why: Unraid keeps its syslog in RAM — after a crash or a hard reset nobody can read what happened, Ms. Protocolli included. Unraid can keep it itself: «⟦Mirror syslog to flash⟧» for a while{wear}.

where.adv.vm_windows.title.one: A Windows VM can hold up the array stop: {names}
where.adv.vm_windows.title.other: {n} Windows VMs can hold up the array stop: {names}

where.adv.vm_windows.why.one: Well, well — when the array stops, Unraid asks every VM to shut down and waits up to {timeout} s (⟦Settings⟧ → ⟦VM Manager⟧ → «⟦VM shutdown time-out⟧»); whatever still runs then is switched off hard, like pulling the plug — unsaved work is gone, and Windows checks its disk at the next start. No guest agent answers in this one, so Unraid's request is the power button — and an idle Windows with its display off likes to ignore it: the array stop waits the whole {timeout} s for nothing, then comes the plug. What helps, in Windows: the QEMU Guest Agent (on the virtio-win ISO: guest-agent\qemu-ga-x86_64.msi) — Unraid then asks the agent, and Windows listens; or in its power options «Turn off the display: Never» and «When I press the power button: Shut down». A longer time-out doesn't help against that — the wait only gets longer; and it has to stay below the disks' shutdown time-out ({disk} s, ⟦Settings⟧ → ⟦Disk Settings⟧ → «⟦Shutdown time-out⟧»).
where.adv.vm_windows.why.other: Well, well — when the array stops, Unraid asks every VM to shut down and waits up to {timeout} s (⟦Settings⟧ → ⟦VM Manager⟧ → «⟦VM shutdown time-out⟧»); whatever still runs then is switched off hard, like pulling the plug — unsaved work is gone, and Windows checks its disk at the next start. No guest agent answers in these, so Unraid's request is the power button — and an idle Windows with its display off likes to ignore it: the array stop waits the whole {timeout} s for nothing, then comes the plug. What helps, in Windows: the QEMU Guest Agent (on the virtio-win ISO: guest-agent\qemu-ga-x86_64.msi) — Unraid then asks the agent, and Windows listens; or in its power options «Turn off the display: Never» and «When I press the power button: Shut down». A longer time-out doesn't help against that — the wait only gets longer; and it has to stay below the disks' shutdown time-out ({disk} s, ⟦Settings⟧ → ⟦Disk Settings⟧ → «⟦Shutdown time-out⟧»).

where.adv.vm_sparse.title.one: A VM disk far bigger than what it holds: {names}
where.adv.vm_sparse.title.other: {n} VM disks far bigger than what they hold: {names}

where.adv.vm_sparse.why: Well, well — {example}. On the server that costs nothing: a sparse file, the empty part isn't stored. But Kopia reads the whole file once, at its first upload, the empty part as zeros — hours for nothing (a 1.6 TB disk holding 21 GB: close to three hours at 200 MB/s); later runs skip the file while it is unchanged. A smaller virtual disk, or a qcow2 disk the guest trims (discard='unmap' on the disk in the VM's XML, then TRIM inside the guest), keeps the file at what it holds. The local snapshots don't mind either way.

where.adv.vm_netmodel.title.one: A VM's network runs through QEMU: {names}

where.adv.vm_netmodel.why: Good to know: with Unraid's network model «virtio-net» every packet of the VM goes through the QEMU process. Unraid recommends it as the default because it is more stable — and for most VMs it is plenty. Only when a VM needs a lot of throughput (several Gbit/s between VM and server; measured: one stream 2.2 Gbit/s with «virtio-net», 93 Gbit/s with «virtio») is «virtio» worth it: ⟦VMs⟧ → the VM → ⟦Edit⟧ → «⟦Network Model⟧». The VM must be off for it; Unraid calls «virtio» faster but possibly less stable.
where.adv.write_method_keep.title: Write method {method} — the right one here
where.adv.write_method_keep.why: «⟦Tunable (md_write_method)⟧» is set to {method}: to write to the array with parity, Unraid first reads the old data and the parity — only the target disk and the parity disk spin, writing is slower. «⟦reconstruct write⟧» (turbo write) reads all the other data disks instead: much faster, but every array disk spins up. None of your shares writes straight to the array — {moved} So only the mover writes to the array, when nobody is waiting for it. {disks}

where.adv.write_method_keep.moved.one: {n} share lands on a pool first; the mover takes its files to the array later.
where.adv.write_method_keep.moved.other: {n} shares land on a pool first; the mover takes their files to the array later.

where.adv.write_method_keep.sleep: And the other disks sleep on. Keep it as it is.
where.adv.write_method_keep.awake: Turbo write would gain nothing there anyone notices. Keep it as it is.

where.adv.write_method_turbo.title.one: A share writes straight to the array: {names}
where.adv.write_method_turbo.title.other: {n} shares write straight to the array: {names}

where.adv.write_method_turbo.why: «⟦Tunable (md_write_method)⟧» is set to {method}: for every block Unraid first reads the old data and the parity, then writes both — only the target disk and the parity disk spin, but big copies take their time. «⟦reconstruct write⟧» (turbo write) reads all the other data disks instead and writes much faster — but every array disk spins up. With no pool in front, what you copy there goes straight onto the array. {disks} {how}
where.adv.write_method_turbo.sleep: Your disks spin down when idle, so turbo write all the time would wake all of them for every little write — use it for big copies: «⟦reconstruct write⟧» before, «⟦Auto⟧» again after.
where.adv.write_method_turbo.awake: Your disks never spin down anyway — as long as that stays so, «⟦reconstruct write⟧» costs you nothing extra and makes those writes faster.
where.adv.write_method_turbo.plugin: Or let the plugin «CA Auto Turbo Write Mode» (⟦Apps⟧) switch for you: turbo write while all disks are spinning anyway, the slow way while some sleep. Or give those shares a pool in front, and the mover writes later.
where.adv.write_method_turbo.plugin_off: The plugin «CA Auto Turbo Write Mode» is installed, but its automatic switching is off — with «Enable Automatic Turbo Mode» on its page it switches for you: turbo write while all disks are spinning anyway, the slow way while some sleep.
where.adv.zfs_arc_passthrough.title: The VM {vm} needs all its RAM at once — ZFS's cache may be in the way
where.adv.zfs_arc_passthrough.why: The VM {vm} has a device passed through (PCI passthrough), and such a VM takes all its {vm_memory} at once when it starts. With the other running VMs ({others}), the containers ({containers}) and Unraid itself only {left} of your {ram} are left — and ZFS's read cache (ARC) may grow to {arc_max} ({percent} % of the RAM; ⟦Tunable (zfs_arc_max)⟧: {setting}). The ARC gives RAM back when it is needed, but bit by bit: a VM that wants everything at once may fail to start, or the kernel ends a container to make room. As a rule «⟦Unlimited (Dynamic)⟧» is right — here I would cap it: ⟦Tunable (zfs_arc_max)⟧ → «⟦Custom value (GB)⟧», e.g. {cap} GB (the RAM minus the VMs, the containers and 4 GB for Unraid, rounded down). Or keep that much RAM free for the VM: zfs_arc_sys_free={sys_free} added to the line «options zfs …» in /boot/config/modprobe.d/zfs.conf (from the next restart).
where.adv.security.title: Security is the night watchman's job now
where.adv.security.why: Shares open to everyone, Telnet, FTP, privileged containers, the CPU's protection — that's his department now, and he notices when something changes, too. Only: he doesn't work here yet. The team lead can hire him. If you ask me: I would.
section.partners_sub: Copies of partner offices whose partnership has ended — the door kept them under <pool>/UnraidSecretaryOffice-partners, nobody receives into them any more.
cat.partners.leftover_text: No pair of that id any more
cat.partners.dropped_text: The pair is still there — the Team Lead no longer keeps this unit of it

park.text_partners.one: This partner's copies go into my storeroom:
park.text_partners.other: These {n} partners' copies go into my storeroom:

park.where_partners: Each stays on its pool: the dataset is renamed into the pool's partners' place (zfs rename — a whole pair next to itself, a single unit one level up, as .UnraidSecretaryOffice-trash-…; its units and snapshots go along), the note of where it came from lies in my storeroom on the flash. Only renamed, nothing is copied — put back any time until you empty the storeroom.
help.partners_text: A partner office kept its copies here (the door received them into <pool>/UnraidSecretaryOffice-partners/<pair>). When the partnership ends the copies stay — dust, but you never know: maybe you pair again. Once the pair is gone from the Team Lead's list I show them here and put them into my storeroom on request (zfs rename next to it) — never while the door is receiving for that pair. I never wake a sleeping disk unless you want me to.
why.transfer_text: The partner door is receiving into it right now — I wait until it's done.
errors.cleanup_partner_transfer: The partner door is receiving into {name} right now — I wait until it's done.
pa.where: Copies of partners whose partnership has ended — the pairs themselves are the Team Lead's.
pa.text: Nothing receives into it any more: the Team Lead has no pair of this id. Should you pair again, a new pair gets a new id — these old copies don't come back on their own.
pa.dropped_text: The partnership with {name} goes on, but the Team Lead no longer keeps this unit for it («Keep less of {name}…»): the door receives nothing more into it, the copies just lie here. I put it into my storeroom on request — renamed into the partners' place on the same pool, put back any time; never while the door is receiving it.
where.partners.title: Partners' copies
where.partners.gone_text: Pair {id} is gone from the Team Lead's list — a leftover in «Tidying up».

where.partners.pair_text.one: {name}: copies of 1 unit, received through the door
where.partners.pair_text.other: {name}: copies of {n} units, received through the door

where.partners.stored_text: Copies of ended partnerships I put away — they are in «Tidying up» → storeroom.

remove.text_kept.other: These {n} volumes go into my storeroom ({size}):

remove.volumes_kept.one: The volume goes into my storeroom first: I copy what it holds (owners and permissions included) beside Docker's data, then Docker removes it. «Put back» there brings it back; only «Empty» deletes it.
remove.volumes_kept.other: The {n} volumes go into my storeroom first: I copy what they hold (owners and permissions included) beside Docker's data, then Docker removes them. «Put back» there brings them back; only «Empty» deletes them.

remove.done_kept.one: Done — the volume is in my storeroom.
remove.done_kept.other: Done — {n} volumes are in my storeroom.

vol.for_good_text: Driver {driver}, or mounted from elsewhere (NFS, CIFS, a folder): what it holds doesn't lie in Docker's folder, so I can't keep a copy — removing it is for good.
restore.done_volume: {name} is a Docker volume again, with everything it held.
errors.cleanup_volume_no_place: I can't tell where Docker keeps its data, so there's no storeroom beside it — {name} stays in Docker.
errors.cleanup_volume_no_space: Not enough space for a copy of {name} in {path}: {need} needed, {free} free — it stays in Docker.
errors.cleanup_volume_copy_failed: Copying {name} into my storeroom failed, so it stays in Docker: {detail}
errors.cleanup_volume_back_failed: Putting {name} back into Docker failed — the copy stays in my storeroom: {detail}
errors.cleanup_volume_exists: Docker already has a volume named {name} — I won't copy over it. Remove or rename that one first.
